text: Philip Leder (November 19, 1934 – February 2, 2020) was an American geneticist born in Washington, D.C., who studied at Harvard University and graduated in 1956. He completed his medical education at Harvard Medical School in 1960 and finished his medical residency at the University of Minnesota. From the 1960s through the 1990s, Leder made significant contributions to molecular genetics, immunology, and the genetics of cancer. He is best known for his early work with Marshall Nirenberg in determining the genetic code through the Nirenberg and Leder experiment. His team defined the base sequence of the complete mammalian beta globin gene, revealing its detailed organization including associated control signals. His research on antibody gene structure was pivotal in explaining how a limited number of genes generate the vast diversity of antibody molecules. This work was later extended to the study of Burkitt's lymphoma, a tumor of antibody-producing cells involving the oncogene c-myc, which was crucial in understanding the tumor's origin. In 1988, Leder and Timothy Stewart received the first patent for a genetically engineered animal—a mouse with genes injected into its embryo to increase cancer susceptibility, known as the "oncomouse," used in cancer therapy research. In 1968, he led the Biochemistry Department of the Graduate Program at the National Institute of Health; in 1972, he became director of the Laboratory for Molecular Genetics at the same institution, a role he held until 1980. He then returned to Harvard Medical School in 1980 as the founder of the Department of Genetics, holding the John Emory Andrus Chair. He retired from this position in 2008 and died of complications from Parkinson's disease on February 2, 2020. Leder was a member of the National Academy of Sciences, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and the Institute of Medicine. He received numerous honors, including the Golden Plate Award of the American Academy of Achievement in 1981, the Lasker Award in 1987, the National Medal of Science in 1991, the Harvey Prize, and the Heineken Prize from the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences. In November 2015, he was awarded an honorary doctoral degree from the Medical Faculty of the University of Basel for his lifetime achievements.
